unitDescription.value: In this unit, students develop practical metalworking and design skills through the construction and redesign of a sheet-metal carryall. Students learn about workshop safety, risk assessment, tools, manufacturing processes, material properties, forces and cold working. Using the SBC Design Model, they investigate existing products, generate ideas and develop an improved carryall for a specific purpose. Students communicate their final solution through sketches and a fully dimensioned SketchUp model.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

description.value: Students complete a two-part assessment consisting of workshop theory and a design folio. The theory component covers safety inductions, risk assessment, the hierarchy of controls, tool identification, material properties and forces. For the design folio, students redesign the carryall for a specific use while retaining its original overall dimensions. Evidence includes background research, brainstorming, an isometric concept sketch, self-evaluation and three PDF views of a fully dimensioned SketchUp model that clearly communicates the proposed improvements.

activities.title: WHS Terminology Match
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach workshop safety terminology using St Brendan's College workshop context. Define 'Hazard' (an object or situation with potential to harm), 'Risk' (the likelihood and severity of harm occurring), 'PPE' (equipment worn to protect against hazards), and 'Control Measure' (an action or engineering control to eliminate or reduce risk). Model an authentic workshop example: 'A sharp, burred edge on a sheet of galvanised steel is a hazard. The risk is a deep laceration to your hand while picking it up. Wearing leather handling gloves is a PPE control; deburring the edge with a file is an engineering control.' Direct students to open their workbooks to the WHS match table.
activities.studentsDo: Read each term in the left column. Select the matching definition from the scrambled bank at the bottom and record the corresponding letter in the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each WHS term to its correct definition using letter codes (A–D) from the bank.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the critical difference between a hazard and a risk in our metalwork shop?
expected: A hazard is the physical source of potential harm (like raw sheet metal edges), while risk is the probability and consequence of that harm actually occurring.
question: Why is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) positioned at the bottom of the hierarchy of controls?
expected: PPE only places a barrier between the worker and the hazard; it does not eliminate the danger and relies entirely on correct human usage.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
(A) An object or situation with the potential to cause harm or injury.
(B) The likelihood that a hazard will cause harm, combined with the severity of that harm.
(C) Equipment or clothing worn by an individual to mitigate exposure to workplace hazards.
(D) An action, procedure, or physical modification implemented to eliminate or minimise risk.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed and eyes on the demonstration bench. Rear-of-room teacher positioning during student completion.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that we are moving from core safety terminology to auditing personal workshop compliance in 60 seconds.

activities.visibleInstructions: Verify each PPE item against SBC workshop standards. Tick the box for each standard you currently satisfy.
activities.questioning:
question: Why are standard canvas school shoes prohibited in the metalwork shop even if they cover your toes?
expected: Canvas provides no impact protection from dropped steel tools or penetration resistance against sharp offcuts.
question: What mechanical hazard is created by loose hair or unrolled long sleeves around rotating equipment?
expected: They can be caught in revolving drill chucks or spindles, causing severe entanglement injuries.

- Eye protection: AS/NZS 1337 certified safety glasses with side shields.
- Footwear: Closed leather upper school shoes/boots.
- Hair & Clothing: Long hair tied behind collar; sleeves rolled above elbows; aprons fastened.

lessons.learningGoal: Demonstrate the safe setup, operational sequence, and hazard controls for the cordless drill and pan brake.

orientate.smartStart: Identify the primary mechanical hazard associated with sheet-metal work on a drill press or cordless drill when the metal is held by hand instead of clamped.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can demonstrate safe operation and safety checks for the cordless drill and pan brake

activities.title: Equipment Safety Checkpoints
activities.teacherDoes: Deliver explicit demonstration at the teacher demonstration bench. Model the 'Cordless Drill Safety Check': (1) inspect chuck jaws and hand-tighten bit centred on flutes; (2) select low-gear speed (1) for metal drilling to avoid work hardening; (3) secure scrap metal to timber backing board using a G-clamp. Model the 'Pan Brake Scan': (1) check sheet thickness capacity (max 1.2mm); (2) verify counterweight arc is clear of bystanders; (3) confirm fingers remain outside clamping blade pinch zones. Articulate thinking: 'I clamp the sheet because the drill bit flutes can snatch thin steel, transforming the scrap into a spinning blade.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, noting specific safety checkpoints for both machines. Complete the structured checkpoints table in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the Equipment Safety Checkpoints table by recording the required action for each listed machine component.
activities.questioning:
Why must sheet metal always be clamped to a timber backing board before drilling? Expected: Thin sheet metal easily catches on the drill bit flutes as it breaks through, causing it to spin dangerously if not clamped.
What happens to the temper of a high-speed steel (HSS) drill bit if operated at excessive speed in metal? Expected: Friction generates excessive heat, annealing the bit, causing it to lose its cutting edge and dull immediately.
activities.scaffolding:
Drill Checkpoints:
- Chuck: Tightened firmly by hand; bit straight in 3-jaw chuck.
- Gear Selector: Set to Low Speed (Gear 1) for higher torque and controlled cutting.
- Clamping: G-clamp sheet firmly to timber scrap on bench.
Pan Brake Checkpoints:
- Clamping Bar: Lock fingers away from edge; use clamping handle smoothly.
- Bending Beam: Ensure operator path and swing radius are clear.
activities.eLearning: Stand around the perimeter of the demonstration bench behind safety tape. Laptops remain in bags.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'In 30 seconds we move to workbenches in pairs to execute the Cordless Drill Induction Checklist.'

workbookSpec.title: Machine Safety Checkpoints
workbookSpec.prompt: Record the mandatory safety action or operational requirement for each machine component.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

2. Drill Speed / Clutch: Select Gear 1 (low speed) for steel; set torque collar to drill mode.
3. Workpiece Clamping: Fasten sheet metal securely with G-clamp to timber backing block.
4. Pan Brake Clamping Fingers: Keep hands outside yellow pinch zone; lock clamping bar lever firmly.
5. Pan Brake Bending Beam: Verify arc of swing is clear of people and foreign objects before lifting.

activities.title: Cordless Drill Practical Induction
activities.teacherDoes:
Supervise students at paired benches. Guide students through physical drill handling: battery insertion/removal, locating the trigger lock, setting speed 1, inserting a 3.5mm HSS drill bit into the keyless chuck, and clamping scrap sheet metal with a backing board. Circulate and provide immediate corrective feedback on clamping rigidity and perpendicular drill stance.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: Watch how I engage the trigger safety lock first. Now, holding the chuck collar firmly, I rotate the sleeve clockwise until the 3.5mm HSS bit is centered and secured with an audible click-tighten. Notice my stance: feet shoulder-width apart, torso upright, applying axial load directly over the drill centerline.
activities.studentsDo: Work with a partner to execute the cordless drill verification steps. Tick each competency item on the checklist as you demonstrate it under teacher observation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Perform each drill setup step on scrap material. Tick each item on your induction checklist once successfully demonstrated.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do we locate and engage the trigger lock switch whenever changing a drill bit?
expected: It isolates the trigger to prevent accidental activation while hands are handling the chuck and cutting edges.
question: Why must downward pressure be reduced slightly just as the drill bit breaks through the underside of the sheet?
expected: To prevent the cutting lips from grabbing the jagged breakthrough burr and snatching the workpiece.
activities.scaffolding: Step-by-step drill handling: 1. Engage trigger safety lock; 2. Open chuck jaws; 3. Insert bit straight; 4. Ratchet chuck closed; 5. Set gear 1 (low); 6. Clamp scrap over timber; 7. Align 90 degrees; 8. Drill at steady moderate RPM.
activities.eLearning: Follow along with the physical workstation requirements. Keep benches clear of unnecessary equipment.
activities.transition: Clean drill shavings into waste bins using bench brushes, return drills to racks, and gather at the pan brake station.

activities.title: Pan Brake Operation Sequence
activities.teacherDoes:
Oversee student execution of test bends on 0.6mm scrap galvanised strips at the pan brake station. Monitor student hand position behind the clamping blade and smooth two-handed lifting of the bending beam. Instruct students to document the sequential folding process using the workbook flow template.

Modelled Example:
1. Pre-check: Verify gauge <= 1.2mm and swing path clear.
2. Load & Align: Slide sheet under clamping fingers and align bend line.
activities.studentsDo: Complete a 90-degree test fold on scrap galvanised steel under teacher supervision. Complete the sequential flow diagram in your workbook detailing the 4 stages of safe pan brake operation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 4-stage flow sequence for making a safe 90 deg bend in the pan brake using the provided technical prompts.
activities.questioning:
What safety risk occurs if your helper places their hand on the machine bed while you pull the clamping lever?
Expected: Severe crushing or amputation of fingers beneath the clamping fingers.
Why must you inspect the metal gauge before inserting it into the pan brake?
Expected: Forcing material thicker than machine capacity (1.2mm) will spring the clamping beam or fracture the machine cast hinges.
activities.scaffolding:
Pan Brake Stages:
1. Pre-check: Verify gauge <= 1.2mm and swing path clear.
2. Load & Align: Slide sheet under clamping fingers and align bend line.
3. Clamp: Pull clamping handle down until lever cams over centre and locks.
4. Bend: Lift bending beam with both hands to target angle, then lower and release.

lessons.title: Precision Marking-Out Techniques on Sheet Metal
lessons.learningGoal: Apply precision marking-out techniques on galvanised sheet metal using a steel rule, engineer's square, and scriber to within 0.5mm accuracy.

orientate.smartStart: Explain in one sentence why using a carpenter's pencil is unsuitable for marking layout lines on sheet metal compared to an engineer's scriber.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can use a steel rule and scriber to mark accurate lines for sheet metal fabrication

activities.title: Marking-Out Tool Geometry & Setup
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'Measure Twice, Scribe Once' protocol. Show students how to establish a datum (reference) edge on a scrap sheet of galvanised steel. Model holding a steel rule on edge to avoid parallax error. Model dragging the scriber at a 75° inclination angled slightly away from the rule edge: 'If I hold the scriber vertically or tilt it inwards, the hardened point wanders underneath the rule, gouging an inaccurate line.' Model using an engineer's try square with the stock held flush against the datum edge.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration of datum edge alignment and scriber angle. Complete the tool callout diagram in the workbook, identifying the correct orientation and angles for precision marking.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the scriber angle, steel rule placement, and datum reference edge on the marking-out diagram using the numbered callout legend.
activities.questioning:
What is parallax error when reading a steel rule, and how do we eliminate it? Expected: Viewing measurement graduations from an angle makes marks appear shifted; we eliminate it by looking perpendicular (directly overhead) or standing the rule on edge.
Why must you scribe each line only once with firm, steady pressure? Expected: Multiple passes create double lines ('tram tracks'), which cause confusion during subsequent folding and cutting operations.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Layout Principles:
- Datum Edge: The true reference edge from which all measurements originate.
- Rule Orientation: Read rule directly perpendicular; align 0mm line, never worn rule ends.
- Scriber Angle: Lean approx. 15° in direction of travel, tilted slightly away from rule face.
activities.eLearning: Demonstration conducted at workshop bench. Laptops stowed.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'Collect your steel rule, scriber, and engineer's square from the shadow board and meet at your assigned vice station.'

workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

2. Steel Rule: Graduations aligned on edge to avoid parallax.
3. Scriber: Tilted 15° away from rule and 75° in direction of travel.
4. Engineer's Square Stock: Pressed firmly against datum edge to guarantee a 90° line.

activities.title: Guided Marking Accuracy Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through marking three target parallel lines on scrap galvanised sheet metal: 15mm (hem allowance), 35mm (box depth), and 75mm (base dimension). Circulate through the workshop benches with vernier calipers to measure student scribed lines against target dimensions, teaching students how to self-audit variance. Model how to align the steel rule zero-mark precisely with the datum edge and how to hold the scriber at a 60-degree angle trailing away from the rule to prevent line drift.
activities.studentsDo: Clamp scrap metal flat on the bench. Use steel rule and scriber to lay out 15mm, 35mm, and 75mm lines from the reference edge. Measure actual scribed distances and record variance in the workbook audit table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Mark target lines at 15mm, 35mm, and 75mm from your datum edge. Measure your actual scribed distances and record the difference in your audit table.
activities.questioning:
prompt: If your actual measurement is 16.5mm on a 15.0mm hem line, what impact will that 1.5mm error have on the folded carryall?
expected: The folded hem will be too wide, overlapping corner clearances and preventing proper assembly alignment.
prompt: Why is it important to use an engineer's square rather than measuring two points and joining the dots?
expected: The square guarantees a true 90-degree line relative to the datum edge, preventing cumulative angular distortion across the sheet.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Tolerance Band:
- Excellent: Variance within ±0.5mm
- Acceptable: Variance within ±1.0mm
- Requires Re-marking: Variance > 1.0mm

Measurement Technique:
- Always align the rule graduation directly over the reference edge.
- Keep the scriber tip pressed lightly against the rule edge to ensure line straightness.
activities.eLearning: Active bench monitoring; students use steel rules and vernier calipers at physical vices.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'Wipe down scrap metal offcuts, store scribes safely in blocks, and open your workbooks to the reflective evaluation.'

activities.title: Hierarchy of Controls Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the 5 tiers of the Hierarchy of Controls using metalwork examples. Explain: 'Elimination physically removes the hazard; Substitution replaces it; Engineering controls isolate people from it; Administrative controls change how people work; PPE protects the individual worker.' Model the distinction between an engineering control (e.g. machine guarding or deburring a razor edge) and PPE (e.g. wearing cut-resistant gloves).

activities.questioning:
q: Why is PPE positioned at the bottom of the Hierarchy of Controls?
Expected: It is the least effective control because it does not eliminate the hazard and relies entirely on worker compliance and correct fit.
q: How does an engineering control differ from an administrative control when managing sharp metal edges?

Compression: A mechanical force that presses, pushes, or squeezes a material, tending to shorten it or cause buckling.
Shear: Unaligned forces acting parallel to a material surface in opposite directions, causing adjacent layers to slide past one another.

activities.title: Structural Geometry and Resisting Buckling
activities.teacherDoes: Present a live physical comparison between a flat 0.6mm galvanised steel strip and an identical strip folded into an L-channel. Place a 500g weight on both to demonstrate how the flat strip buckles immediately, while the folded section supports the load effortlessly. Explain that adding a flange redistributes the cross-sectional area further from the neutral axis, dramatically raising the moment of inertia and resisting buckling under compression. Guide students through the cloze notes in their printable workbook.

activities.questioning:
question: Why did the flat sheet buckle under the test mass while the folded strip remained rigid?
expected: The fold creates a three-dimensional flange that increases the moment of inertia, giving the cross-section structural depth to resist bending.
question: What risk occurs if we clamp the pan brake too tightly on 0.6mm sheet?
expected: Excessive clamping pressure can crush the galvanised coating or induce shear stresses along the bend line.

- flange (a projecting flat rim or lip formed by folding)
- clamping bar (upper mechanism of the pan brake that secures the workpiece)
- shear (parallel cutting force)

activities.title: Teacher Demonstration: Pan Brake Setup and Safety Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the pan brake. Model the complete pre-operational safety check: verifying clearance around the counterweights and checking fingers for burrs. Demonstrate how to adjust the clamping fingers to accommodate 0.6mm galvanised sheet without binding. Align a scribed line with the clamping nose, check sightlines, clamp the metal firmly using the clamping lever, and lift the folding leaf smoothly to 90 degrees plus 2 degrees to compensate for spring-back. Model checking the internal angle with an engineer's square.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, noting machine parts, pinch point zones, and sequential clamping steps on their Pan Brake Safety and Operation Checklist workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration at the pan brake. Tick off each operational safety step on your workbook checklist as it is modelled by the teacher.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do we bend the sheet slightly past 90 degrees before releasing the clamping bar?
Expected: To account for elastic spring-back in the galvanised steel, which causes the metal to return 1 to 2 degrees after release.
q: What constitutes a severe pinch hazard when operating the pan brake?
Expected: Placing fingers between the clamping fingers and the bed, or between the folding leaf and the clamping bar during the sweep.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist items to observe and verify:
1. Area clearance: 1-metre exclusion zone around counterweights.
2. PPE verification: Safety glasses worn, sleeves rolled up, hair tied back.
3. Finger alignment: Clamping nose perfectly parallel to the scribed fold line.
4. Clamping tension: Secure grip to prevent slippage without crushing material.
5. Controlled sweep: Smooth, two-handed lift of the folding leaf.
6. Spring-back compensation: Over-bending by ~2 degrees.
7. Inspection: Engineer's square flush against both folded faces.
activities.eLearning: Ensure students keep physical distance around the pan brake demonstration line.

activities.teacherDoes: Pair students at the pan brake stations. Supervise students performing test bends on 0.6mm galvanised steel offcuts. Model an adjustment for spring-back: 'Notice how the steel relaxes slightly when we release the leaf; we must pull fractionally past 90 degrees to account for elastic recovery.'

- Benefit: The functional advantage, strength enhancement, or safety improvement delivered to the user.

- Swaged rib -> Prevents panel oil-canning and compressive buckling under load.

Instruction also covers technical specifications for drilling, including the selection of high-speed steel (HSS) bits and the calculation of appropriate drilling speeds for thin-gauge steel.

This week bridges the gap between conceptual thinking and physical manufacturing through isometric drawing and pop-riveting. The classroom environment emphasizes the importance of structural integrity and the aesthetic quality of mechanical joins in professional metalwork.

resources.value: Pop rivet guns, 3.2mm aluminium rivets, G-clamps, isometric grid paper, 2H pencils, technical drawing equipment, partially assembled carryall components.

theory.value: Explicit teaching on the principles of isometric drawing, focusing on the use of 30-degree axes to represent the carryall in a three-dimensional view. Students learn how to represent hidden detail and exploded views to clarify how their design improvements integrate with the standard chassis. The theory of permanent joining is introduced, specifically the mechanics of blind (pop) riveting. Students investigate why riveting is preferred over welding for thin-gauge galvanised steel, considering the preservation of the protective zinc coating and the avoidance of heat distortion.

In the workshop, they begin the final assembly by securing the end panels to the main body using pop rivet guns. Emphasis is placed on the use of G-clamps to maintain structural alignment before drilling through both layers of metal simultaneously. Students evaluate each rivet for a 'flush fit,' ensuring the mandrel has snapped correctly and the joint is under sufficient tension to prevent movement.

Establish the overall bounding envelope of the carryall chassis (length, width, height) using light 2H construction lines. 2. Show how every vertical fold line follows the vertical grid lines. 3. Demonstrate projecting the 15mm folded end-panel flanges along the 30-degree receding grid lines. 4. Explicitly model drawing dashed lines for internal hidden flanges and rivet centre-marks. Why do we crate the entire carryall into a light bounding box before drawing specific folds and handles?
Expected: Crating ensures the overall height, width, and length remain in correct proportion and prevents lines from drifting off the 30-degree axes.
What is the convention for representing internal structural edges that cannot be seen from the outside?
Expected: Dashed lines of medium weight with consistent dash lengths.

2. HB pencil for visible object outlines.
3. Dashed lines (---) for hidden edges and rivet centres.
4. Text annotations with straight leader lines.

lessons.title: Carryall End Panel Assembly and Pop Riveting
lessons.learningGoal: Apply blind pop riveting techniques to permanently join sheet-metal carryall end panels to the chassis ensuring structural alignment and flush mechanical joins.

orientate.smartStart: On your workbench, inspect the 3.2mm aluminium blind rivet, cordless drill fitted with a 3.2mm bit, and pop rivet gun. Identify the three safety hazards present when drilling and riveting sheet metal and list the control measure for each in your workbook.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can safely drill and pop-rivet carryall end panels to the main chassis with correct alignment and flush joints

activities.title: Workshop Safety and Blind Riveting Operation
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central demonstration bench. Demonstrate personal protective equipment (safety glasses mandatory). Model the mechanical assembly sequence: 1. Align the end-panel flange tightly inside the chassis fold. 2. Secure both components firmly using two G-clamps with scrap timber pads to avoid surface indentation. 3. Hold the cordless drill perpendicular (90 degrees) to the metal surface and drill a 3.2mm hole through both thicknesses simultaneously. 4. Insert the 3.2mm aluminium rivet body fully into the hole until the flared head is completely flush. 5. Slide the rivet gun nozzle over the mandrel, keep the nozzle flat against the head, and squeeze the handles steadily until the mandrel snaps. Model common faults: gap under rivet head caused by loose clamping, and oversized hole caused by wobbling the drill.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration closely from the safety boundary. Complete the procedural quality checklist in their workbooks as the teacher demonstrates each operational stage.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the assembly demonstration. In your workbook, review the Quality & Safety Checklist steps that must be verified before and during mechanical joining.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must we drill through both layers of sheet metal simultaneously while clamped, rather than drilling each panel separately?
expected: Simultaneous drilling guarantees identical hole alignment, preventing shear misalignment and eliminating oval holes that cause loose rivets.
q: What does it indicate if the rivet head spins or has a visible gap between itself and the metal surface after snapping?
expected: The clamp was loose during drilling or the rivet gun nozzle was not held perpendicular and tight against the rivet head when squeezed.
activities.scaffolding:
Assembly Sequence Checkpoints:
1. Clamp: Minimum two G-clamps positioned within 50mm of the joint.
2. Drill: Cordless drill held at exactly 90 degrees; 3.2mm high-speed steel bit.
3. Deburr: Remove swarf with bench brush, never bare hands.
4. Insert: 3.2mm rivet pushed until head sits flush.
5. Squeeze: Firm, progressive stroke until mandrel snaps.
6. Clean: Drop spent mandrel directly into the scrap tin.
activities.eLearning: Workshop environment; laptops and devices stored away in cubbies.
activities.transition: Put on your safety glasses, move to your designated workshop vices, and prepare your practice scrap strips for guided test riveting.

workbookSpec.title: Blind Riveting Quality and Safety Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify each safety and procedural condition before performing rivet assembly on your carryall chassis.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 9 checklist items must be ticked by the student and verified during teacher floor checks before students drill their final project chassis.
items: Safety glasses inspected and worn over eyes.
Sheet-metal flanges aligned and secured with two G-clamps.
Cordless drill bit checked for 3.2mm diameter and tightened in chuck.
Drill held at strict 90-degree angle to prevent oval or oversized holes.
Metal swarf cleared using a bench brush (never bare fingers).
Rivet flange seated completely flush against sheet surface prior to pulling.
Rivet gun nozzle held firmly down against rivet head during compression.
Mandrel snaps cleanly at calibrated point under tension.
Spent mandrel collected and placed into metal recycling bin.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 9 checklist items must be verified and checked off by the instructor during floor monitoring prior to authorizing students to proceed with drilling and riveting their structural components.

activities.title: Guided Practice: Clamping, Drilling, and Setting Test Rivets
activities.teacherDoes: Distribute two pre-cut scrap strips of 0.6mm galvanised sheet metal to each student pair. Walk students through the guided execution: 'Step 1: Overlap the strips by 15mm. Clamp them tightly with a G-clamp. Step 2: Teacher check on clamp security. Step 3: Drill one 3.2mm hole. Step 4: Insert the rivet and snap the mandrel.' Provide immediate corrective coaching on tool grip, perpendicularity, and body positioning. Model a correct test rivet on the whiteboard: show a flush head, zero gap, and a clean mandrel break.
activities.studentsDo: In pairs at workbenches, clamp practice metal strips, drill a 3.2mm pilot hole, and operate the rivet gun to set a permanent joint. Inspect the test joint for tension and flushness, and complete the quality continuum rating in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Clamp practice strips with 15mm overlap using a G-clamp.
2. Drill one 3.2mm hole perpendicular to the sheet.
3. Insert 3.2mm rivet fully.
4. Compress rivet gun until mandrel snaps.
5. Complete the joint quality rating and justification in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
q: If you feel the drill bit grabbing aggressively as it punches through the second sheet, what should you do?
Expected: Ease back on feed pressure and keep the drill speed high to prevent the sheet from catching and spinning or warping the metal.
q: How do you test if your riveted joint has sufficient mechanical tension?
Expected: Attempt to twist the joined strips by hand; there should be zero rotational play, and no gap should be visible beneath the rivet head.
activities.scaffolding:
Tactile feedback cues:
- Drill sound: High pitch, steady hum without stalling.
- Gun feel: First squeeze draws mandrel tight; second squeeze snaps mandrel cleanly.
- Joint inspection: Flat, tight, no rattle.

activities.teacherDoes: Supervise independent assembly of carryall end panels to the main chassis. Monitor the workshop perimeter ensuring: safety glasses remain on, work is clamped before drilling, and spent mandrels are not left on the floor where they create slip hazards. Check each student's structural squareness using an engineer's square across the chassis corners before they rivet the second side. Model how to check for a flush rivet head using a steel rule edge across the face.
activities.studentsDo: Independently assemble both end panels to their carryall chassis: align panel flanges, clamp securely with two G-clamps, drill 3.2mm holes through both layers, and insert and set pop rivets on both left and right sides. Log assembly quality checks in the workbook table.

1. Position end panel inside chassis fold.
2. Apply two G-clamps to secure flange alignment.

5. Record your quality verification in your workbook table.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it vital to check the chassis for squareness before setting the rivets on both ends?
Expected: Once rivets are set, the joint is permanent. If the chassis is twisted or out-of-square, it cannot be adjusted without drilling out all the rivets.
question: If a rivet fails to snap properly or remains loose, how must it be removed?
Expected: Carefully centre-punch the rivet head and drill out the rivet body using a 3.2mm drill bit without enlarging the parent metal hole.
activities.scaffolding:
Step-by-step assembly protocol:
1. Fit end panel 1 -> Clamp left & right flanges -> Verify 90-degree squareness -> Drill & rivet.
2. Fit end panel 2 -> Clamp left & right flanges -> Verify 90-degree squareness -> Drill & rivet.
3. Total fasteners: 8 rivets (4 per end panel).
4. Inspect: Run finger over joint (watch for sharp swarf) to verify flush fit.

activities.questioning:
question: What occurs to the crystalline structure of galvanised steel strap if it is bent back and forth repeatedly in a bending jig?
expected: Cold working causes work hardening, increasing hardness while significantly decreasing ductility, resulting in embrittlement and cracking.
question: Why must a dry-fit be verified with clamps before riveting?
expected: Blind rivets are permanent mechanical fasteners; any misalignment of holes under tension will cause shear stress and deform the chassis.

activities.title: Functional Stress Testing and Failure Mode Analysis
activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate the standardized functional load test: 1. Place a calibrated 5 kg test weight inside the chassis; 2. Lift carryall by the handle grip for 15 seconds; 3. Apply moderate lateral (side-to-side) displacement (approx. 20 N force); 4. Inspect for rivet shear, joint separation, or handle deflection. Model how to document observations objectively and translate physical joint deformation into digital redesign requirements.
Example Script: 'When we apply the 5 kg vertical load, look closely at the blind rivet heads. If the shank begins to elongate or tilt within the clearance hole, note this as 'bearing deformation' in your audit table. We will then translate this exact physical failure into our upcoming SketchUp models by adding structural stiffening hems.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct the 5 kg vertical load and lateral force tests on their assembled carryall. Observe joint behaviour, identify any elastic or plastic deformation, and record observations and design rectifications in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions:

2. Lift by handle grip for 15 seconds; record any deflection.
3. Apply gentle lateral force; check for rivet rotation or joint loosening.
4. Complete the Structural Performance Audit table.

question: Under vertical loading, what mechanical stress is primarily applied to the rivet shank?
expected: Shear stress across the interface between the handle tab and the chassis wall.
question: If the chassis sidewall flexes outward when lifted, what CAD design feature should be incorporated to reinforce this area?
expected: Introduce a folded stiffening hem, rolled bead, or triangular reinforcing gusset in the digital model.

activities.teacherDoes: Model the application of the SketchUp 'Dimensions' tool on the projected chassis model. Demonstrate placing linear, radial, and overall bounding-box dimensions. Explicitly show the standard convention: dimension text and lines must sit outside the object silhouette, with extension lines offset from object geometry to prevent visual clutter. Script: 'Watch how I select the two corner vertices, drag the leader line out by 10mm, and lock the dimension text in parallel projection. If I place it across the sheet metal face, a fabricator will confuse fold lines with dimension witness lines.'

prompt: Why must dimension lines be placed outside the model's perimeter profile?
Expected: Placing them outside prevents dimension lines from obscuring visible edges, bend lines, or hole centres, ensuring manufacturing clarity.
prompt: What error occurs when dimension text is aligned vertically or upside down in an orthogonal drawing?
Expected: It breaches Australian CAD drafting conventions, forcing the reader to turn the drawing and increasing the risk of fabrication errors.
activities.scaffolding:
CAD Dimensioning Rules:
1. Units: Metric millimetres (mm) implied without writing 'mm' repeatedly.
2. Clearance: Keep dimension lines at least 5–10 mm clear of component edges.
3. Hierarchy: Place smaller internal feature dimensions closest to the object; place overall length/width/height furthest out.
4. Projection: Always switch camera to Parallel Projection and standard Views (Top, Front, Right).

activities.title: Demonstrating Push-Filing and Edge QC Standards
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate push-stroke filing and abrasive finishing on exposed 0.6mm galvanised sheet-metal edges at the vice. Explicitly explain: apply uniform forward pressure, lifting the file slightly on the return stroke to avoid dulling teeth and producing chatter marks. Demonstrate testing for geometric squareness using an engineer's square held against the chassis base and fold return. Show how to detect burrs safely using a scrap cotton rag (snag test) rather than bare fingers. Script: 'Observe the angle of the smooth-cut file. I am holding it at 45 degrees along the edge. If I drag backward, I create burrs and strip the protective zinc coating unnecessarily.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration from the safety perimeter wearing eye protection. In workbooks, complete the vocabulary and QC standard matching table to reinforce finishing terms before handling tools.

activities.questioning:
q: Why does dragging a metal file backward across sheet steel damage both the tool and the workpiece?
Expected: Dragging backward bends and blunts the forward-facing cutting teeth and creates chatter ridges on the thin sheet metal.
q: Why must students avoid excessively sanding or grinding the surface of galvanised steel?
Expected: Aggressive abrasion removes the sacrificial zinc coating, exposing the bare mild steel beneath to rapid atmospheric corrosion and rust.
activities.scaffolding:

- Burr: A sharp, raised edge or sliver of metal remaining after cutting, shearing, or drilling.
- Flush Joint: A mechanical seam where two connecting sheet faces sit perfectly level in the same plane.
- Engineer's Square: A precision measuring tool used to verify 90-degree internal and external angles.
- Galvanising: A metallurgical zinc coating bonded to steel to provide sacrificial corrosion resistance.

activities.title: Technical Vocabulary of Manufacturing Documentation
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the three core concepts of production documentation: Technical Annotation, Manufacturing Tolerance, and Assembly Sequence. Show an example of an incomplete CAD drawing versus one with industry annotations. Script: 'Geometry shows the shape; annotations provide the specification. An annotation specifies that the sheet is 0.6mm zinc-annealed steel and that fasteners are 3.2mm aluminium blind rivets. Without these callouts, a contractor could use 2mm steel and steel rivets, ruining the weight and causing galvanic corrosion.'

activities.questioning:
Why are dimensions alone insufficient for a third-party fabricator to manufacture the carryall? Expected: Dimensions show physical size, but they do not communicate material alloy, sheet thickness, hole drill sizes, rivet types, or surface finishing treatments.
What is the purpose of specifying a manufacturing tolerance like ±0.5 mm on sheet metal folds? Expected: It defines the acceptable range of dimensional variation, preventing parts from being rejected for minor, non-critical discrepancies while ensuring fit.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Reference:
- Technical Annotation: Textual notes, leaders, and symbols added to drawings to detail materials, tooling, fasteners, and finishing specs.
- Manufacturing Tolerance: The permissible limit of variation in physical dimensions from the nominal design size (e.g. ±0.5mm).
- Assembly Sequence: The chronological, step-by-step order in which individual components are folded, drilled, and fastened together.

question: Why must test loads be lowered gradually rather than dropped into the carryall?

activities.teacherDoes: Guide paired groups through applying calibrated 5kg and 10kg loads. activities.studentsDo: Work in pairs to place 5kg and then 10kg test masses into the carryall tray. Measure and record base deflection in millimetres using steel rules. Visually inspect rivet joints and chassis seams for signs of shear or buckling, recording data into the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions:

4. Remove weights and check if the base returns to zero deflection (elastic limit check).
activities.questioning: If the base returns to its original position after the 10kg mass is removed, what does this tell us about the metal's elastic limit? Expected: The applied stress remained within the elastic range of the sheet metal and did not cause plastic deformation. What visual sign indicates that a rivet has experienced shear stress beyond its allowable limit? Expected: The rivet shank tilts, the hole elongates into an oval, or daylight appears under the rivet head.
activities.scaffolding:

- Observations to note: 'Rivet firm', 'Minor base flex', 'Permanent fold crease', 'Handle elongation'.

activities.title: Material Science and Mechanical Terminology Match
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly review core material science and mechanics concepts relevant to the carryall unit. Model the distinction between terms: 'Malleability enabled us to fold the 0.6mm sheet metal without cracking along the seam. Ductility allowed the rivet mandrel to pull and expand the rivet sleeve. Work hardening occurred along every pan-brake bend, increasing local yield strength.' Instruct students to match each term to its precise technical definition.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each material science term in the left column with its correct engineering definition from the definition bank below the table.
activities.questioning: Why did the sheet metal become stiffer and more resistant to bending precisely along the 90-degree fold line? Expected: Cold working in the pan brake created dislocations in the metal's crystal structure, causing work hardening. How does shear stress differ from tensile stress in the carryall handle assembly? Expected: Tensile stress acts along the length of the handle pulling it apart, while shear stress acts across the rivet cross-section perpendicular to its shaft.
activities.scaffolding:
Reference Definitions:
- Work Hardening: The strengthening of metal through plastic deformation at room temperature.
- Malleability: The ability of a material to deform under compressive stress without fracture.
- Shear Stress: Opposing forces acting parallel to a plane, attempting to slide adjacent surfaces apart.
- Tensile Stress: Forces pulling along the axis of a material tending to stretch or elongate it.

activities.title: Evaluation Terminology and Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define 'Design Criteria', 'Constraints', 'Tolerance', and 'Design for Manufacture' (DfM) in sheet-metal engineering. Write out the definitions on the whiteboard. Model how each term applies directly to the carryall: 'For our chassis, the 0.6mm thickness and overall dimensions were non-negotiable constraints, whereas deburring quality and rivet spacing of +/- 1mm were design criteria and tolerances.' Rear-of-room visual scan to ensure workbooks are open.
activities.studentsDo: Match each evaluation term to its correct definition in the workbook table by writing the corresponding letter from the bank.

activities.questioning:
Why is 'tolerance' critical when folding and riveting sheet-metal components? Expected: Tolerances ensure folded seams align and pre-drilled holes overlap flush without inducing shear stresses or warping.
How does a 'constraint' differ from an evaluative 'design criterion'? Expected: A constraint is an inflexible limitation such as material stock or machinery limit, while a criterion is a standard used to judge how well the solution performs.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Design Criteria: Specific functional and aesthetic benchmarks used to evaluate the success of the product.
- Constraints: Inflexible boundaries or limitations such as material dimensions, budget, or tool capacity.
- Tolerance: The allowable amount of dimensional variation (+/- mm) from a specified measurement.
- Design for Manufacture: The engineering practice of designing products so they are easy and efficient to fabricate with available tools.

workbookSpec.title: 3-2-1 Project Evaluation Reflection

activities.title: Workshop Maintenance Standards and Lubrication
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the professional decommissioning and maintenance procedure for metalworking tools. Model the safe removal of swarf from bench shears and the pan brake bed using a natural-bristle bench brush—never bare hands or compressed air. Demonstrate applying two drops of light machine oil to the pivot bolt of hand shears, working the mechanism, and wiping away excess oil with a clean rag to prevent swarf accumulation. activities.questioning:
question: Why must compressed air never be used to clean metal swarf off workbenches and machinery?
expected: Compressed air propels sharp metal particles at high velocity, creating severe eye and skin puncture hazards.
question: What is the purpose of wiping away excess machine oil after lubricating tool pivots?
expected: Excess oil attracts abrasive dust and swarf, creating a grinding paste that accelerates joint wear.
activities.scaffolding:
Maintenance Procedure:
1. Debris clearing: Hand brush only; sweep swarf into scrap pan.
2. Inspection: Check cutting jaws for chips, burrs, or loose pivot bolts.
3. Lubrication: Light machine oil on pivot pin; cycle tool 5 times.
4. Wiping: Clean lint-free rag to remove oil film on handles and outer faces.
5. Inventory: Align tool with matching silhouette on shadow board.

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All seven items must be ticked to confirm a complete and correctly formatted design folio submission.
items: Initial Design Brief and user requirements documented
Three dimensioned SketchUp views included with AS 1100 annotations
Completed Quality and Safety Audit sheet included
Three high-resolution photographs embedded (Isometric, Top-Down, Macro)
3-2-1 Evaluative reflection completed with engineering justification
File exported as a single PDF and named SBC_Year8_Tech_LastName_Carryall.pdf
Upload completed and green submission confirmation screen verified
